title: A Quarter of Recently Deceased NFL Players Had CTE
hook: CTE can only be diagnosed after death, which has made its true prevalence a guess. A new study of former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 puts the floor at 25%.
key_points: At least 25% of former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE.
CTE is a degenerative brain disease linked to repeated head impacts.
It can currently only be diagnosed by examining brain tissue after death.
Earlier estimates came from donated brains, which over-represent symptomatic players.
This study's design makes 25% a floor rather than a headline maximum.
Repeated sub-concussive hits, not just diagnosed concussions, appear to matter.
content_html: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy has been linked to football for well over a decade, but a basic question stayed unanswered: how common is it? The obstacle is diagnostic. CTE can only be confirmed by examining brain tissue after death, and most published series relied on brains donated by families — who tend to donate precisely when the person had troubling symptoms. That selection inflates the rate and made the resulting numbers easy to dismiss.
extra_html:
This study takes a different cut: former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021, of whom at least 25% had CTE. The design matters more than the number. Because it starts from a defined group of deaths rather than a donation pipeline, 25% functions as a floor — the true figure for that population is likely higher, since not every brain was examined.

The wider point for anyone not playing professional football is about exposure. The evidence increasingly implicates repeated sub-concussive impacts — the ordinary hits of a season that never get diagnosed as anything — rather than concussions alone. That reframes the risk from "did you get knocked out" to "how many years of routine head contact," which is the question youth and amateur leagues are now weighing.

related.title: Keeping Your Brain Healthy
related.hook: No pill prevents dementia, but the habits that protect your heart turn out to protect your brain too.

related.title: Nearly Half of Dementia Risk Is Something You Can Change
related.hook: A long-term brain study tied smoking, high blood pressure, heart disease, and high blood lipids to the damage behind vascular dementia — risks that are all treatable.

flashcards.prompt: Why has CTE prevalence been so hard to pin down?
flashcards.back_html: It can only be diagnosed by examining brain tissue after death, and most earlier studies used donated brains — families donate when symptoms were present, skewing the rate.

flashcards.prompt: How should the 25% figure be read?

choices.text: As a floor — at least a quarter of those who died in that window had CTE
As the exact lifetime risk for any football player
As the share of current NFL players with symptoms

flashcards.explanation_html: The study covered former players who died 2016–2021 and reports at least 25%. It's a lower bound for that group, not a universal risk estimate.

flashcards.prompt: Is CTE risk only about diagnosed concussions?
flashcards.back_html: No. The evidence points to repeated sub-concussive impacts — routine hits that never get diagnosed — as a major part of the exposure.
